20350-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for September 1864, volume fourteen, number eighty-three, appeared mid-Civil War. One essay warns of a gradual, general increase of insanity in the land. Statistics reveal that rise, it says, to any who care to look. A provident people should weigh what unchecked growth might bring.

If sanity is a glory all might lose unawares, the essay asks. Then all should ask if they are in their wits at this moment. Such grave pieces sat beside poems and tales in the Monthly. Readers get a stark window on wartime America's anxious mind.
21009-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
A born Londoner of part Italian stock defines his ground in The Atlantic Monthly for February 1866. A government clerk by trade, he writes with a traveller's roving eye besides. Volume seventeen, number one hundred opens with his frank self-portrait.

The Atlantic Monthly set America's literary tone from its Boston home. Essays, tales, poems, and reviews of high polish fill each monthly number. This February issue came as the nation healed from civil war. Its pages show the magazine at work, binding a bruised republic back together with letters, thought, and art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldassare-pe: This 1913 reference article on Baldassare Peruzzi — the Sienese architect and painter. Gerhard Gietmann praises his graceful works. His Villa Farnesina charms all Rome. St. Peter's felt his planning hand. The elegant master of the High Renaissance. His perspective deceived the Roman eye.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-gozzi: A 1913 entry on Carlo Gozzi — the Venetian playwright of the fairy tales. Jeremiah Ford honors his fiabe. His Turandot charmed the age. He warred with Goldoni's reform. The champion of the old comedy. His Love of Three Oranges is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-m: A 1913 entry on Cardinal Madruzzi — the Bishop of Trent. Francis Schaefer honors his council's part. He hosted the fathers at Trent. The empire prized its prince-bishop. The host of the great council. His Trent palace hosted the fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cola-di-rienz: This 1913 reference article on Cola di Rienzi — the Roman tribune. Umberto Benigni honors his brief glory. He dreamed the ancient republic's return. The Capitol crowned his fleeting power. The last of the Roman tribunes. His Santo Spirito rising is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-bar: A 1913 entry on Francesco Bartolozzi — the Florentine engraver. Leigh Hunt honors his famous stipples. His burin graced the London press. The Academy prized its gifted son. The prince of the English engravers. His 1764 London is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-mel: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Francesco Melzi — Leonardo's beloved pupil. George Williamson honors his faithful discipleship. He inherited the master's precious papers. Milan knew the devoted heir. The keeper of the Vinci manuscripts. His 1570 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-xavie: This 1913 reference article on Francis Xavier Patrizi — the Jesuit exegete. Walter Drum honors his famous commentaries. His pen illumined the sacred text. The order prized its learned son. The doctor of the Roman schools. His 1881 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-martin: This 1913 reference piece on Martinuzzi — the great Hungarian churchman — tells his mighty tale. Johann Peter Kirsch wrote it up. He ruled the Transylvanian land. Assassins struck the fearless chief. His 1551 murder is famed. His red hat is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto: A 1913 entry on Cavazzi — the Capuchin of Congo. Lawrence Hess honors his famous Istorica. His pen chronicled the African missions. The scholars mine his vivid pages. The historian of the Congo missions. His 1678 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-cozz: A 1913 entry on Cozza-Luzi — the Basilian scholar. Umberto Benigni honors his famous works. His pen served the Vatican library. The order prized its learned son. A monk among the editors. His 1905 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-lanzi: A 1913 entry on Lanzi — the Jesuit art historian. Gerhard Gietmann honors his famous Storia. His pen ordered the Italian schools. The galleries prized the weighty tome. The eighteenth century knew his name. His 1810 death is famed. His 1792 Storia is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-mozzi: A 1913 entry on Mozzi — the Jesuit writer. Andrew MacErlean catalogs his works. Little is known of his career. The eighteenth century was his era. The order prized its learned son. His 1790 works are famed. His 1790 writings are famed. His 1790 Jesuit pages are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-migazzi: A 1913 entry on Migazzi — the Vienna cardinal. Cölestin Wolfsgrüber notes his famous see. Few details of his life remain. The eighteenth century was his age. Austria knew his name. His 1803 death is famed. His 1757 Vienna is famed. His 1757 imperial see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piazzi: Giuseppe Piazzi was the monk-astronomer who discovered the asteroid Ceres in 1801. This entry covers his career, his observatory at Palermo, and his fame. The priest who found a new world: his tiny Ceres opened the vast asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-pompon: Pomponazzi was the Paduan philosopher who denied the soul's immortality could be proved by reason. This entry covers his career, his doctrines, and his condemnation. The scandal of the Renaissance schools: his daring De Immortalitate shocked learned Padua to its core.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-mary-ma: St. Mary Magdalen de' Pazzi was the Carmelite mystic of Florence. This entry examines her ecstasies, her counsels, and her fame. The bride of the Florentine cloister: her rapt ecstasies moved the city of Florence in the 1580s' convent of the Carmelites.
podcast-dannyjones-YnDW4ythQZI:
Former LSD kingpin Seth Ferranti shares his secrets with Danny Jones in this episode. Ferranti ran a major acid distribution network as a young man, then served a long federal prison sentence. He came out a writer, telling the story of the acid empire's rise and fall.

Ferranti describes how the LSD trade worked at its peak, from chemists to street dealers. He covers the manhunt, the trial, and the decades behind bars that followed. Jones asks what that life cost him and what he learned. Curious listeners get a wild life told straight by the man who lived it.
podcast-joerogan-xEBeQH39CZI:
Fighter Aljamain Sterling headlines Rogan's MMA Show number 184. Sterling held a top title with a grappling-heavy style. His wrestling base made him a hard puzzle for rivals.

Rogan breaks down Sterling's fights and ground game in detail. They talk about cuts, camps, and the cost of each camp. Sterling explains how he studies rivals on tape. The episode suits fight fans who love the chess side of the sport: grips, scrambles, and the small choices that decide who leaves with a belt. His calm in talk contrasts with his cage pressure.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-11-sep:
Eloquence opens the September 1858 Atlantic. Music masters teach that whoever can speak can sing, the essay begins; so, too, every man is eloquent once in his life. Men differ only in the heat at which they boil.

One man catches fire in parlor talk, with a shallow two-inch zeal. Another needs a crowd and a public debate, a third an opponent or hot anger, a fourth a revolution. A fifth needs nothing less than the grandeur of pure ideas, heaven and hell themselves. A crowd, the essay adds, catches the flame from one speaker and turns hearers into conductors of the charge.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-23-sep:
The life and works of Ary Scheffer lead the September 1859 Atlantic. No painter of the age, the writer claims, has pressed so deep on the popular mind of America. Few living artists are so at home at American firesides, known and loved in the remotest towns.

Few of Scheffer's own canvases have been shown in the country, yet engravings from them are familiar to every person of taste. Young maidens love their tender sadness, the essay says, and suffering hearts find comfort in their pure, high faith. Such an effect must have a cause, and the writer finds it in the aim and character of the artist himself, whose two leading traits the piece goes on to name.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-35-sep:
Among the Trees leads the September 1860 Atlantic. Whoever studies trees, the essay begins, must be struck by their worth, not only for the beauty of a landscape but for the whole economy of life. In no other part of the plant world has Nature done so much for the comfort, food, and shelter of her creatures.

Trees house wild animals and feed them in large part. Man in a state of nature weaves his tent from their branches and thatches it with their leaves. He hunts in their shades for flesh and furs, and takes from their wood the tools to catch his prey. His earliest meal-food, too, came from trees.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-47-sep:
The Shakespeare Mystery leads the September 1861 Atlantic. In 1853, the essay recalls, a joyful cry rose at the printing of Mr. Collier's Notes and Emendations to the text of Shakespeare's plays, drawn from early manuscript corrections. Doubt and strife, it was said, were at an end.

The shout had hardly died before a counter cry of warning rose from a few firm lips. Growing mouth by mouth, it drowned the first. The fight over the margin readings in that famed volume has now ended. Nearly all the readings peculiar to it have been rejected. The verdict also goes against any show of authority in them at all.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-59-sep:
David Gaunt, a story, leads the September 1862 Atlantic under a German motto from Goethe's Faust about the spirit of the times. It opens by asking what sort of sword old Christian carried in his famous fight with Apollyon, long ago. He cut the fiend to the marrow at last, the writer recalls, though the battle went hard with him for a time.

Some of Christian's blood, Bunyan says, is on the stones of that valley to this day. The strange little valley fades back from the sober freshness of a summer morning: its lasting twilight, lily-crusted meadows, and herd-boy's quiet song, close upon the borders of hell. Then the view shifts to busy early streets, children racing to school, and willows shimmering in sunlight.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-71-sep:
The Puritan Minister leads the September 1863 Atlantic. The hour is nine on a summer Sabbath morning, in a year of the sixteen hundreds. Sunlight falls on a small forest settlement. Around its growing fields the great American wilderness draws back day by day.

Bears, wolves, and Indians withdraw ever farther off. Yet the stout wooden gates closing the village street at both ends keep their meaning. The place would look busy and thriving today but for the Sabbath stillness brooding over it in almost excess of calm. Smoke rises more faintly than usual. Since three o'clock the day before, worldly work has wholly stopped.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-110-de:
December 1866 leads with John Pierpont. Most men of fourscore and upward, the essay says, who have been mightily abused in their day are found on close inquiry to have long outlived themselves. Here is a man who, in his eighty-second year, kept his edge to the very last.

He held the temper of a Damascus blade, the writer says. Its bright blue rippling glitter stayed with him. Or rather, he held the temper of that strange tool found among the ruins of Thebes. That tool was once used to smooth and polish. The piece sums up a long, fighting life at its close, measuring how a poet and reformer stayed sharp when age dulls most men.
